title: Let it go: How trusted reminders alter intention maintenance
research_question: Does experience with reminders of different perceived reliability cause people to shift from internally maintaining prospective intentions to relying on external reminders?
methodology: The authors ran a two-session prospective-memory experiment with 320 university students using a 2 × 3 × 2 mixed design crossing session, reminder reliability (0%, 50%, or 100%), and reminder availability at retrieval. Participants encoded prospective-memory word pairs while performing a lexical-decision task, and intermittent thought probes during the retention interval measured whether they were thinking about the prospective-memory task, the ongoing task, or unrelated material. Session 1 established experience with reminder support, while Session 2 manipulated expected reliability and unexpectedly withheld reminders from some participants. Three-way ANOVAs and corrected post-hoc tests were reported with effect sizes, confidence intervals, and Bayes factors.

key_findings.finding: During the initial trust session, reminders improved prospective-memory performance without reducing prospective-memory-related thoughts, which is consistent with duplicative rather than immediately substitutive offloading.

After experience with reliable support, participants expecting 100% reliable reminders reported substantially fewer prospective-memory-related thoughts than both the no-reminder and 50%-reliability groups.
The 100%-reliability condition also produced more ongoing-task-related thoughts, while reminder reliability did not meaningfully alter task-unrelated thought.
When reminders remained available in Session 2, both reminder groups substantially outperformed the no-reminder group in prospective-memory accuracy.

When expected reminders were unexpectedly absent, the 100%-reliability group performed worse than the no-reminder group, but the associated Bayes factor was equivocal, so the authors characterize this result as suggestive rather than definitive.

Participants in the 50%-reliability condition continued to maintain prospective-memory-related thought, and their unaided performance did not fall below the no-reminder condition when reminders were withdrawn.

limitations: The retention intervals were brief and reminders were imposed by the experimenter, limiting ecological validity for long-lived real-world intentions.
Thought-probe categories were mutually exclusive, so increases in one category necessarily redistribute responses away from other categories.
The participants were university undergraduates rather than workers managing naturally occurring obligations.
The experiment examines individual prospective intentions rather than longitudinal cross-thread work-item states such as new, open, resolved, or superseded items.
It does not evaluate obligation-versus-preference selection or joint omission, repetition, and false-alert outcomes.
Forty-nine participants received invalid response options on one post-experimental verification question, although most had independently demonstrated target detection.
raw_claims: The final analyzed sample contained 320 participants.
The design manipulated reminder reliability at 0%, 50%, and 100%.
Thought probes were collected before retrieval and served as a real-time measure of conscious intention maintenance.
Reminder groups showed enhanced prospective-memory performance during the initial trust session without fewer prospective-memory thoughts.
In the critical session, the 100%-reliability group reported fewer prospective-memory-related thoughts than the other reliability groups.
The 100%-reliability group reported more ongoing-task-related thoughts in the critical session.
Task-unrelated thought did not show meaningful pairwise differences across reminder-reliability conditions.
Unexpected withdrawal of a fully trusted reminder produced a small, statistically significant but Bayes-factor-equivocal accuracy decrement relative to no reminders.
Data, materials, and analysis scripts are provided through the Open Science Framework.
